chapter.title: Two C libraries side by side: musl and glibc

section.title: Why two C libraries
section.para: Every dynamically linked program on Linux is bound to one C library: its ELF header names that library's dynamic loader, and its code calls that library's ABI. The two C libraries in wide use are not interchangeable:

listitem.para: The C library of most Linux distributions. Prebuilt software — commercial applications, games, vendor SDKs and drivers, many language runtimes and their binary packages — is published for glibc and does not run on musl.

section.para: On an FHS system both would compete for /lib, /lib64, /usr/include, the loader path, ldd and the compiler. DHS gives each its own directory and rules for which programs use which, so a system can be musl-based and still run glibc software without either breaking the other.

section.title: Primary and secondary C library

listitem.para: The primary C library is the one the base is built against. On a DHS system it is musl. It is part of the base layer.
The secondary C library is glibc. It is an ordinary userland package: the user installs it when glibc software is needed, and removing it leaves the base untouched.

section.para: The base layer MUST NOT contain files linked against the secondary C library. A base upgrade MUST reject such files.

section.title: Directories
section.para: Each C library is installed into a directory named after its GNU target triplet:

row.entry: lib/libc.so.6 and the other glibc libraries
bin (ldd, iconv, locale, …), not on PATH
gcc, g++, cc, c99 and arch-vendor-linux-musl-gcc
libstdc++, libgcc_s in the base lib
its own copies in the glibc lib

section.title: The shared directories belong to the primary C library
section.para: The secondary C library MUST NOT install anything into the shared bin, sbin, lib or include of the system view. As a result cc, the headers in the default search path, ldd and every library in /overlayer/syshub/lib are musl's, and installing glibc changes none of them.

section.title: Every program names its own loader
section.para: The ELF interpreter (PT_INTERP) of every dynamically linked program MUST be the DHS path of the loader of the C library it was linked against. A program therefore always starts with the right loader, whichever C libraries are installed.

section.title: Library search paths do not cross

listitem.para: The musl loader searches, in this order, /overlayer/syshub/lib, the musl lib directory and /overlayer/zexlib/union/lib. Base programs also carry /overlayer/syshub/lib as their library path (RPATH).

The glibc loader MUST search only the glibc lib directory and the directories listed in its own etc/ld.so.conf. It MUST NOT search /overlayer/syshub/lib: the libraries there are built for musl and cannot be loaded into a glibc process.
Libraries that glibc programs need — including the C++ runtime — are installed into the glibc lib directory.

section.title: Both C libraries read the same system configuration
section.para: Users, groups, passwords, host names, DNS and the time zone are system facts, not library facts. The paths compiled into the secondary C library MUST point at the base:

row.entry: /etc/passwd, group, shadow, hosts, resolv.conf, nsswitch.conf, localtime

section.para: The secondary C library SHOULD be built with these paths changed by source patches, so that no symbolic links are needed.

listitem.para: The unprefixed compiler names (cc, gcc, g++, c99) MUST belong to the primary C library.

The secondary C library's compiler MUST be installed under its triplet name only, MUST take its headers, start files and libraries from the glibc directory, and MUST write the glibc loader's DHS path into the programs it links.
Each toolchain has its own pkg-config search path, so that a build against one C library never picks up .pc files of the other.
An implementation MAY let the user select which toolchain the unprefixed names run, per shell or as a system setting. The default MUST be the primary C library.

note.title: Implementation note
note.para: On Zainium OS, sys-resolver env glibc prints the environment that makes cc, gcc, g++, cpp and pkg-config use glibc in the current shell; elevate sys-resolver set glibc|musl changes the system default and sys-resolver get shows it. The variable ZAINIUM_LIBC overrides the setting for one command.

section.title: Package managers leave glibc programs as they are
section.para: A package manager that adapts foreign packages to DHS paths () MUST recognise programs and libraries linked against glibc — by their interpreter or their dependency on libc.so.6 — and MUST NOT rewrite their loader or library path to musl's.

row.entry: What goes wrong when both share FHS paths
Both loaders and both libc files compete for /lib and /lib64; a package of one library can overwrite the other's.
Each loader is in its own triplet directory; every program names its own ().
Compiling against one library's stdio.h and linking against the other's libc produces programs that fail at run time.
Each library's headers are in its own include; each compiler is built to use only its own.
A glibc program finds a musl-built libz.so in /usr/lib and crashes or fails to load.
The glibc loader never searches the shared lib ().
libstdc++ and libgcc_s built for one library are loaded by programs of the other.
Each library has its own copies.
ldconfig lists libraries of both in one ld.so.cache.
glibc's cache and configuration live in glibc's directory and list only glibc libraries.
glibc's ldd or iconv replaces musl's and gives wrong answers for base programs.
glibc's tools stay in glibc's bin, off PATH.
A build picks up .pc files of the wrong library.
Two libraries read users, DNS or the time zone from different places and disagree.
A program built on another distribution names /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2, which a DHS root does not have.
The missing loader path is redirected to the installed glibc loader ().
